curriculum.lesson_evidence: We can balance on different body parts, at different levels and in different shapes, such as wide, narrow, curled or stretched. Changing the base of support, the shape and the level makes a balance easier or harder. The aim is to hold a balance still for 3 to 5 seconds and then move out of it smoothly. Partners can make matching or contrasting balances while standing apart, without leaning on each other.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Which balance is easier to hold: standing on both feet, or standing on tiptoe on one foot? Give a reason using the words 'base of support'.

FEEDBACK
Standing on both feet is easier because the base of support is bigger. One foot on tiptoe has a very small base, so tiny movements make you wobble.

WATCH FOR
Believing a balance is only good if it is hard. A good balance is still, controlled and safe at a level that suits you.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Create six different balances using different body parts, levels and shapes, and draw each with a label. Hold each for 5 seconds, order them from easiest to hardest and say why using 'base of support'.

Write a short reflection naming one choice you changed and why. Any movement is optional, adult-supervised and can be done in a gentler way or described instead.
